description: How Hermes runs its own business automation: a Cloudflare-native engine with scheduled jobs, queues and retries, durable receipts, readback checks and a watchdog — with AI as a helper, never the scheduler.

h1: Hermes Automatic Engineer: business automation that runs without a laptop
conciseAnswer: Hermes Automatic Engineer is the internal engine Hermes uses to run its own business automation. Jobs are scheduled and queued in the cloud, retried safely, recorded with receipts and checked against the real system after every write, so work continues when nobody's computer is on and AI never decides on its own when something runs.
explanation: Most small-business automation starts on someone's laptop: a script, a spreadsheet macro or a chat assistant that only works while that person is online. Hermes hit the same wall across Logistics, Marketing, Academy and Hermes Connect, so we built one shared engine instead of another script per task.

The Hermes Automatic Engineer runs on Cloudflare. A thin scheduled tick decides what is due, a queue carries each job and retries it when a provider is slow, and an operational database keeps the job, its events and a receipt of what actually happened. After any write to an outside system, the engine reads the result back, so a job is only marked done when the real system confirms it.

AI is useful inside this flow — drafting, classifying, summarising — but it is never the scheduler or the source of truth. Deterministic rules decide when work runs; AI suggestions pass through the same receipts, checks and owner approvals as everything else. Sending email or changing an account stays off unless an owner approves that specific action.

Every change to the engine follows the same release ladder we use for client work: coded, tested in CI, merged, deployed, verified live and only then counted as done. A health watchdog flags stuck or failing jobs instead of letting them fail silently. Today the engine is private and runs Hermes' own operations; it is also how we design the automation we build for clients in Hermes Technology and Hermes Connect.
takeaways: Run business automation in the cloud, not on one person's laptop
Retry safely and keep a receipt for every job
Read the result back from the real system before calling a job done
Use AI as a helper inside the flow, never as the scheduler
Ship automation changes through the same tested release ladder as product code

title: How US Service Businesses Get Found in Search and Maps | Hermes Insights
description: A source-checked practical SEO and GEO checklist for US service businesses: truthful service pages, Google Business Profile eligibility, internal links and qualified-lead measurement without promises of rankings.
eyebrow: Marketing / Practical guide · 23 October 2026
h1: How service businesses get found: an evidence-first SEO and GEO checklist
conciseAnswer: A US service business improves its chances of relevant discovery by explaining each real service on an accessible page, maintaining accurate public identity, linking original evidence, and measuring how search visitors reach genuine inquiries. For eligible local companies, a complete verified Google Business Profile may help customers find them on Search and Maps. These actions do not guarantee rankings, AI citations or sales.
explanation: Start with a customer decision. A buyer looking for car-hauling dispatch needs equipment fit, onboarding and carrier requirements; a repair shop considering CRM needs the actual service workflow and an understandable contact route. Give each distinct intent one clear canonical owner URL. Explain the offer, real service coverage, what the buyer should prepare and the next step. Educational Insights should answer a different question and point to the commercial page, not duplicate its service text.

Before adding pages, check whether the important ones can be discovered and understood. Use helpful navigation, descriptive links, accurate titles and canonical URLs. Ensure the main content is available to users and crawlers, keep internal links working, and submit a sitemap as a discovery aid. Search Console URL Inspection can show indexing status; a sitemap entry or successful deployment does not prove Google indexed a page. Keep existing case, company and resource pages linked when simplifying the homepage.

For truly local services, identify the place or service area honestly. Google's Business Profile guidance describes relevance, distance and prominence as the main local ranking factors. An eligible storefront or in-person service-area business should verify and maintain its category, hours, coverage, photos and genuine reviews. A remote-only agency or software provider should not invent a public shop address or pretend to have a customer-facing location. Location landing pages need distinct user value, not a city name swapped into a template.

Show proof that belongs to the business. Original case-study details, verified public service descriptions, actual training resources and clear legal identity can make decisions easier. A published screenshot or source document demonstrates only what that source establishes: it does not automatically prove a search ranking gain, booked appointment, revenue result, live software feature or a customer endorsement. For AI-assisted search and geographic discovery, readable and accurate text with clear ownership is more defensible than publishing mass-generated variations.

Use structured data to describe visible facts, not to manufacture them. Organization identity and other applicable schema should match the page and its canonical source. Google's structured-data policy says eligibility for rich appearance is not a guarantee. No schema field guarantees that an AI assistant will cite your brand. Improve page speed, usability and mobile contact paths for the people visiting the website before treating markup as a growth result.

Finally separate discovery from business outcomes. Review Search Console impressions, clicks, country, device and landing pages; then, with appropriate consent and CRM access, follow real CTA actions into qualified inquiries, opportunities and completed services. Compare similar periods and do not turn missing attribution into zero. A jump in impressions is not the same as a sale. Google's own SEO documentation notes that changes may take hours to months and cannot guarantee ranking improvement.

The 2026 Hermes Home redesign illustrates a practical content-retention rule: a concise four-direction entrance can become easier to navigate without destroying valuable company facts, public resources or case-study pages. Those sources stay at their original addresses and are discoverable from Insights. This article is a general implementation framework, not evidence that Hermes or a client achieved a particular traffic or revenue increase.
takeaways: Give each real customer question one useful page and a clear next action.
Verify local Business Profile eligibility and only claim real operational coverage.
Preserve original evidence and canonical links when redesigning.
Measure search visibility separately from qualified inquiries and revenue.
No number of new articles, structured data tags or AI optimizations guarantees rankings.

faq.question: Should I make a landing page for every city and keyword?
faq.answer: Only when your business genuinely serves that audience and the page adds distinct truthful value. Near-duplicate city pages can compete with useful canonical service content.

faq.question: Does Google Business Profile guarantee first place in Maps?
faq.answer: No. Google identifies relevance, distance and prominence as key local factors and does not provide a guaranteed paid shortcut.

faq.question: Will schema markup make AI assistants recommend my business?
faq.answer: No. Markup should describe facts already visible on the page; it does not guarantee rich results or AI citations.

faq.question: Which SEO numbers indicate business value?
faq.answer: Treat impressions and clicks as discovery metrics; inspect relevant inquiries, qualification and source-verified completed sales separately over consistent periods.

title: Hermes Home Redesign: Four Live Video Windows That Stay Fast | Hermes Insights
description: How Hermes rebuilt its home page around four live multi-shot video windows — one per direction — while keeping every film under 1.5 MB, honoring reduced motion and Save-Data, and never breaking cached media.
eyebrow: Technology / Website Release · Hermes Home · 22 October 2026
h1: Four live windows, one fast page: what we changed on the Hermes home page
conciseAnswer: The Hermes home page now opens on four separate live windows — Logistics, Technology, Academy and Marketing — each playing a short multi-shot film of real work. Every film is self-hosted, under 1.5 MB, starts only when its window is visible, pauses off-screen, and falls back to a still poster for reduced motion, Save-Data and no-JavaScript visitors.
explanation: A home page for four different businesses has one job: let a visitor recognise their own direction in a few seconds. We replaced a single shared strip of artwork with four separate rounded windows. Each window carries its direction colour, a one-line description of who it serves, and a short film that cuts between several real scenes — a car hauler on the highway and freight lanes for Logistics, code and a team at the screen for Technology, a trainer and a practice session for Academy, a planning wall and a team meeting for Marketing. The windows remain plain links, so the page still works as navigation before any video loads.

Video is the heaviest thing a page can ship, so the films follow a strict budget. Each runtime file stays under 1.5 MB, uses 540×960 frames for the four-column layout and a 720×1280 variant only where a window is wide enough to need it, carries no audio track and is encoded for fast start. Nothing is fetched from a third-party video CDN at runtime. A film is attached only when its window scrolls into view and pauses again when it leaves, so a visitor reading the contact section is not paying for four videos they cannot see.

Motion is optional by design. Visitors who ask their operating system for reduced motion, browsers that send Save-Data, and sessions without JavaScript all see a still poster frame and the same links. That keeps the page accessible and keeps the visual promise honest: the poster is a real frame from the film, not a different illustration.

One engineering detail matters for any site that ships media. Our media files are cached by browsers for a year as immutable. Re-encoding a film under the same file name would mean returning visitors never see the new version. Every new cut therefore gets a new file name, and the old files stay untouched. The same release also refreshed the four direction pages with clearer headlines, two concrete next steps each and a navigation bar attached to the header.

These are the same rules we apply to client websites at Hermes Technology: a measurable media budget, progressive loading, accessible fallbacks and cache-safe releases, checked by automated browser tests on desktop and mobile before anything goes live.
takeaways: Give each audience its own visible entry point instead of one shared hero
Set a per-file media budget and load video only when it is actually visible
Treat reduced motion, Save-Data and no-JavaScript as first-class experiences
Never change bytes behind a cached media URL — ship a new file name

faq.answer: Each film is under 1.5 MB, self-hosted and loaded only when its window is visible. Off-screen windows pause, and visitors with reduced motion or Save-Data get a still poster instead of video.

h1: Inside the correction loop: attempt, feedback, retry
conciseAnswer: The Hermes Academy method is built on one idea: a single correction should change the next attempt. Learners explain and practise, review their own work first, receive one precise correction from a human reviewer, try again visibly, and then transfer the skill to a changed scenario before a person decides whether they progress.
explanation: Most training measures whether someone finished the material. The Academy measures whether the next attempt got better. That is why the first attempt is treated as evidence, not a verdict: it shows what the learner already understands and exactly where the gap is.

The loop has three movements. Explain and practise: understand the context, explain it in your own words and try the work in realistic scenarios before any live responsibility. Review and retry: name your own gap first, receive human feedback from a reviewer and make a visible second attempt. Transfer and grow: use the skill in a changed situation, ideally without notes, and then pass a human progression gate.

This sits inside the Academy's three learning stages — awareness, understanding and application — and inside a clear participation lifecycle: application, human review, orientation, learning and practice, feedback and quality. Exercises may include scripts, scenarios, documents, recordings, analysis, briefs and revisions when the format supports them.

Progression stays human. A reviewer decides whether a learner should continue, repeat, change direction, pause or complete the approved stage. No certification is represented unless an approved offer defines it, and training does not guarantee employment, income, clients or promotion.
takeaways: A first attempt is evidence of the gap, not a verdict
Self-review comes before one precise human correction
The skill must transfer to a changed scenario before progression
A person, not a score, decides the next stage

title: How the Hermes Load Board Separates Live Freight From Previews | Hermes Insights
description: Why the Hermes car-hauling Load Board keeps approved live records and labelled, non-bookable preview rows in two separate layers — and why the live section is allowed to show zero.

h1: How the Load Board separates live freight from previews
conciseAnswer: The Hermes Load Board has two layers that never mix. The live marketplace shows only approved, active, unexpired public records that pass source, permission, freshness and public-visibility checks — and it may show zero. A separate market preview lets carriers evaluate lane, equipment, deadhead, timing and paperwork, and every preview row is clearly marked and not bookable.
explanation: A load board is only useful if a carrier can trust what it shows. The most common way a board loses that trust is by mixing real loads with examples, stale postings or rows nobody has permission to publish. We designed the Hermes Load Board around one rule: a visitor must always be able to tell what is live and what is an illustration.

The live marketplace is source-gated. A record appears there only when it is approved, active and not expired, and only when the source, permission, freshness and public-visibility checks pass. If nothing passes, the live section says so and shows zero rather than filling the space with something that looks like freight.

The market preview exists for a different job: helping a carrier decide whether a lane is worth their time. Preview rows can be filtered by city, radius and equipment, and they show the inputs a carrier weighs — lane, equipment, deadhead, timing, paperwork, payment terms and carrier approval. Every preview row is labelled as a preview and is not bookable. The RPM and deadhead calculator uses only the numbers the visitor enters and does not claim a live market rate.

Shippers and dealers use the same page to start a vehicle transport request, and carriers move from the preview into the carrier-access workflow. Keeping the two layers apart is what lets the board be honest on a quiet day and useful on a busy one.

title: Organic Social Before Paid Ads: What Meta Data Can Prove | Hermes
description: A public Instagram profile cannot validate CAC, retention or a sales funnel. Hermes explains an evidence-first sequence: internal audit, organic baseline, controlled paid learning, then offer validation.

h1: Why a public Instagram profile cannot validate a paid funnel — and what to measure first
conciseAnswer: Public social profiles can show content, visible engagement and public identity, but they cannot reveal the internal audience, retention, attribution, cost and conversion data needed to validate a paid funnel. Meta says its 2026 ads systems can incorporate additional organic engagement data from Instagram. Hermes therefore uses an evidence-first operating sequence — audit → organic baseline → controlled paid learning → offer validation — as a measurement discipline, not as a claim that Meta requires every business to wait a fixed number of months before advertising.
explanation: Start with the evidence boundary. A public Instagram, Facebook or Threads page can support a useful outside-in audit: content cadence, visible creative patterns, public calls to action, identity consistency and obvious discovery gaps. It cannot honestly prove Reach by audience segment, watch-time retention, non-follower distribution, paid-versus-organic contribution, lead quality, CAC, consultation conversion or revenue attribution. Those decisions require authorized platform analytics and CRM evidence. That is why Hermes Catalog marks public observations, private-analytics requirements and owner-confirmation gaps separately instead of turning a screenshot into a confident funnel recommendation.

Meta's own January 2026 engineering and business update gives an important signal without justifying an overclaim. Meta says its newer ads ranking work uses longer behavior sequences and can incorporate additional organic engagement data on Instagram. That shows organic engagement can be one input in the broader advertising system. It does not say that every company must complete a fixed organic warm-up period, that stopping ads permanently damages an account, or that an organic winner automatically becomes a profitable paid offer. Those stronger claims still have to be tested against the actual account and business economics.

Hermes therefore treats organic programming as a learning layer. Build a repeatable content matrix, measure which hooks, formats and audience themes consistently outperform the account's own baseline, and connect those observations to profile actions, site visits or qualified conversations where possible. Once repeated organic winners exist, use a small controlled paid-learning budget to compare creative and audience response. The purpose is not to scale immediately; it is to collect cleaner evidence about whether the signal survives paid distribution and whether downstream actions remain qualified.

Only after that signal gate should the team call an offer or funnel validated. The offer then needs a canonical destination, explicit CTA, source/UTM capture and CRM stages that connect content → click or message → qualified lead → consultation → sale → delivery outcome. If paid traffic produces cheap clicks but weak qualified actions, the funnel is not working. If a social post produces high views without meaningful next actions, it is a distribution result, not sales proof. This sequence reduces the chance of optimizing vanity metrics while commercial decisions remain unmeasured.
takeaways: Public social data supports an outside-in audit, not a validated CAC or sales funnel
Meta says its ads ranking work can incorporate additional organic engagement data from Instagram
Hermes treats organic baseline → controlled paid learning → offer validation as an evidence discipline, not a universal Meta rule
A real funnel needs internal platform analytics plus CRM attribution from content to qualified action and revenue

explanation: What changed: DAT reported dry-van spot linehaul paid to carriers averaging $2.17 per mile for the week ending September 18, 2026, excluding fuel. The national average fell $0.03 per mile, or 1.2%, from the prior week. At the same time, it remained $0.53 per mile, or 32.8%, above the year-earlier level and $0.36 per mile above DAT's nine-year seasonal average of $1.82. That combination matters because a soft week-over-week move can coexist with a market that is still comparatively firm over a longer horizon.

Why it matters: a single national number is not a lane quote. DAT's regional data for the same week ranged from $2.66 per mile in the Great Lakes and $2.64 in the Ohio River region to $1.42 in Florida–South Georgia. A carrier can therefore see a strong national or origin-region headline while still accepting a movement that produces weak round-trip economics because of destination demand, deadhead, appointment timing or the quality of the next reload.

Historical Hermes operating material repeatedly treated route planning, deadhead reduction, broker negotiation and the next reload as one decision chain. The then-versus-now lesson is not that an old internal rate or earnings target should be reused. It is that the same operating discipline becomes more valuable when the market is moving in different directions across time horizons and regions: verify the lane, understand where the truck lands, and price the full movement rather than one loaded segment.

What to do: use DAT's current market average as an external reference point, then calculate the actual movement. Separate loaded miles from deadhead to pickup and likely repositioning after delivery. Add current fuel and toll assumptions, time requirements, equipment constraints and payment terms. Compare realistic reload options in the destination market before negotiating. A counteroffer is more defensible when it is tied to the truck's real operating picture instead of a national headline alone.

Result: the carrier gets a repeatable decision process instead of a reactive rate rule. The September 21 DAT update says the national dry-van linehaul average eased slightly after a strong year-over-year rise; it does not say every lane is weakening or that every load should target $2.17. The practical outcome is to refresh lane assumptions more often, keep deadhead visible in the calculation, and use current regional context to decide where the national average is useful and where it is misleading.
